text:
PSA: you should get your ferritin (iron stores) tested. Especially women!! And especially if you get (or want to be) pregnant.

I didn’t realize this was an issue for me, because my CBC (complete blood test: measures red and white blood cells, platelets, hemoglobin and hematocrit) results have always good, so doctors have always been happy.

Roughly two years ago, I was feeling a lot of fatigue (and just generally felt off - like my nervous system was out of whack) and went down a health rabbit hole. My ferritin was in the 20s (below 30 ng/mL, you’re considered iron deficient). Doctors were dismissive, but I started taking oral supplements and felt noticeably, shockingly better (physically and mentally) as I gradually reached the 40s.

That’s where I was when I got pregnant late last year.

I started to feel pretty tired in the back half of my second trimester. Maybe this is just what pregnancy feels like? But thanks to DrGPT, I knew that pregnancy is an incredibly iron intensive process, so I asked my OB to check my ferritin. She did a CBC instead, and said everything was fine. I insisted on having my ferritin checked. She finally agreed, and my ferritin was 33 ng/ML, and obviously trending downward.

I’ll spare you the drama, but after a lot of back and forth (and encouragement from a doctor friend that I wasn’t being unreasonable), I got a referral to a hematologist, who agreed we should try to bring my iron stores up. Not only is it important for the pregnancy, but also for breastfeeding and postpartum recovery (which in my experience, no one in healthcare focuses on beyond the six week checkup).

I started doing weekly iron infusions in my third trimester. It took a week or two to kick in, but holy shit! I had my energy back. I felt fantastic during the stretch that’s supposed to be the most draining, all the way up until delivery at 40 weeks. When we last tested, my ferritin was at 122.

In the hospital, multiple doctors and nurses marveled at my excellent CBC results post-delivery. Depleted iron stores can eventually show up in these other results, and some degree of anemia after giving birth seems to be treated as routine, especially given the blood loss.

And while there are a ton of other factors, along with a lot of luck and randomness, I’ve felt pretty great in my first 3.5 weeks postpartum.

Obviously this is just my experience, and health is incredibly personal. But I’ve seen people (majority female - we’re especially susceptible because we lose iron through menstruation) post on reddit and social media about single digit (!!!) ferritin scores and doctors who don’t seem curious or concerned. There's also early evidence linking low ferritin to fertility challenges, and suggesting that addressing iron deficiency may reduce miscarriage rates (there's also speculation that it could improve egg quality).

This has been both a radicalizing and empowering experience for me, and I’ve been spreading the word 1:1…it’s shocking how many friends are dealing with a similar issue. Now that I’m on the other side of the pregnancy, I’m going to spend more time understanding the root cause for my low ferritin (Bryan Johnson seems to be on a similar journey).

Happy to chat if helpful! Get your ferritin checked!

We partnered with Baklavastory, our neighbor in the Mission, to show what it sounds like when a business's character and warmth stay consistent, no matter who calls or what language they speak.

.@fal's Gorkem Yurtseven and Batuhan Taskaya on making an open source video model 35x faster, and what Hollywood wanted after they built it:

Last month, MiniMax released H3, an open source video model. fal rebuilt it - they cut down the steps the model takes to make a video, rewrote the code under each stage, and got the GPUs to 70-80% of their theoretical ceiling instead of their usual 30-40%. No quality loss.

Video now generates faster than you can film it. The models have gotten so cheap and fast that end users aren't even asking for improvements in either category anymore. The gap has moved to quality, or how closely the model follows the prompt.

Hollywood wasn't a customer a year ago and is now fal's fastest growing segment. Studios love it for the little things - extending a shot, moving the camera, changing the lighting. Those edits land 80-90% of the time. fal is chasing 99.9%.

"Amazon MGM Studios, at their conference, released their Project Nara tool. It's mostly backed by fal infrastructure behind the scenes. We are seeing incredible pull coming from Hollywood."

text:
fal's Gorkem Yurtseven and Batuhan Taskaya on how faster-than-real-time generation unlocked continuous, interactive AI video:

"One of our engineers, Rehan, started streaming a live stream of continuous generations of H3 Max from his laptop. He was doing some prompt tricks, trying to keep a coherent story, and then he started livestreaming that on Twitch."

"Our ML team was essentially trying to take every single video model and apply these optimizations and tricks... You never could generate five seconds under five seconds. Once H3 Max unlocked it, the ML team was like, 'This is insane.'"

"You can essentially stream infinitely. We capped it at an hour... I think it's the only model that can generate up to 60 minutes of continuous video that is action-controlled."

"You can start with a prompt, say there's an office setting and someone is working, and then 30 seconds later it just imagines by itself. 30 seconds later, you can say, 'A woman walks in through the door.' It can take the prompt and reflect it immediately, which is the most fun part."

"And the office is still the same office. The camera can pan back to the original person, and the original person is still there in the same state."

@gorkem @isidentical @fal

text: When I talk to nonprofit leaders about AI they often report widespread resistance from staff, usually because of environmental objections (that mix real issues & fake ones). It causes them frustration because they’re all under-resourced for their mission & see AI as a way to help

I had access to the new Claude Projects and was able to do some very complex work.

Here, I asked it to go through all the images, videos and records about Umberto Eco's famous 33,000 book library & try to reconstruct it, including book locations, in 3D. https://eco-library-map.netlify.app/

What makes Claude Projects so interesting is that it handles teams of agents really well, you talk to a main orchestrator agent and it spins up specialists. Basically it creates an organization to solve your issue, mixing expensive and cheap agents depending on your preferences.

For example, I asked Fable in Claude Projects to select famous historical mysteries that it could try to resolve. It initiated research agents, selected the mysteries based on data it could access, and spun up eighteen separate threads, each with an agent each focused on one mystery. Then each thread launched additional agents (simulating avalanches, breaking codes) before summarizing those and passing them to still more agents for write up and another set of skeptical agents to fact check. It did this over a day of work, with the central orchestrator agent organizing it all. 

The results were interesting if you like historical mysteries. They are also for fun and certainly not definitive or guaranteed error-free (but they are also mostly reasonable & grounded in the literature). https://historical-mysteries.netlify.app/

Caveats: I take no money from the AI labs, and pay for my own accounts, but during early access there is no limit on tokens so I can’t speak to costs.

Also, I have published peer reviewed work in history but am only an interested amateur on the topics the AI selected.

this is why capable high intelligence local ai needs to be built into every computer, so ppl who need this technology can access it affordably and sustainably without extraordinary environmental concerns that come with cloud datacenter scaling

text:
I didn't expect people who read and shared a lot of my data center stuff to become more sympathetic to EA, but I have to admit it's been disappointing seeing them share and retweet a lot of flat out lies about what EA is like. So it goes.

In general, we are not at all anti-America, anti-capitalist, consumed with guilt, technophobic, socially rewarding each other for being as doomy as possible, living crazy lifestyles, or relying on some ridiculous religious belief in infinitely powerful AI. These are memes about us mostly developed by people who haven't interacted with the broad scene for a long time and are just inferring that we must be like any of the other people they don't like. There are individual examples of people into EA who do fall into each category, because there are so many people who are into it, but people are lurching from those individuals to say the whole scene is the same. It's not at all.

If you've enjoyed my past work, I don't ask you to give EA any more sympathy than you think it deserves, but I do ask that you not wildly misrepresent me and my general scene based on the memes that are flying around right now.

@venturetwins @QuiverAI The attention to detail... I was mesmerized watching it create the svg lol. 

What screen recording tool did you use to capture the footage/edit? Very well done!

Okay I'll take the bait! 😅 

I appreciate and respect your work around data centers and think the point you've brought up is worth addressing. 

IMO there 3 of the key reasons that EA is getting this reaction: 

1) The groupthink is strong + feels judgmental to outsiders. Many folks feel it's hard to communicate with EAs if you don't share their beliefs because they're such deeply held moral judgments and backed up by the strength of the group. It's like EA is a fringe religion that (sometimes) thinks their beliefs should apply to everyone, which makes people nervous.

2) Some of the beliefs (especially around AI safety) aren't backed by data. It often feels tough to get a clear answer from folks about why they believe certain things. There's no logical chain of thought to follow or engage with, it's just a vibe of vague panic and people telling you to read "If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies."

3) The loudest voices are often pretty weird. Since there's no clear leader, when people think of EA and rationalists (which are obviously broadly confused w/ each other), they think of SBF, Aella, and Yudkowsky. Or the random polyamory drama that often spills into the timeline in a dramatic way a few times a year. Just doesn't give the impression it's a group of serious people.

Having said that - I don't condone the ad hominem attacks on peoples' appearances, for example. I think that's uncalled for. But I don't believe EAs do the best marketing for themselves...
